title: How Eco-anxiety Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss eco-anxiety, a proposed condition of chronic fear of environmental doom (global warming, floods, extinction) with symptoms similar to generalized anxiety. They connect the eugenics movement and voluntary sterilization by two women concerned about population and the environment to eco-anxiety, cover eco-psychologists' explanation that it stems from disconnection from nature, eco-therapy advice (carry a rock or bark, go outside, at about $250 per session), skepticism about the diagnosis, the role of media such as An Inconvenient Truth in fueling it, and fear-uncertainty-dread (FUD) as a marketing tactic. The episode closes with a "useless information" segment on why scaring a vulture is a bad idea, and a pointer to related articles on HowStuffWorks.

segments.title: Opening and eugenics history
segments.summary: Josh opens the show and introduces eugenics, the early twentieth-century American movement that led to sterilization of people deemed deficient, and notes Henry Ford's support and its influence on Hitler. He then mentions two women who voluntarily sterilized themselves to avoid adding to population and environmental harm.

segments.title: Defining eco-anxiety
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh define eco-anxiety as chronic fear of environmental doom such as global warming, floods, famine, heat waves, or extinction, with symptoms like insomnia, nervousness, and depression. They describe people obsessing over cans and bottles and sifting through trash for recyclables, and compare this to hobos.

segments.title: Anxiety as a general trait and polling
segments.summary: The hosts suggest eco-anxiety may be a trigger for general anxiety, comparing it to historical fears like fear of flying and claustrophobia. They cite a Gallup poll finding 36 percent of Americans worry a great deal about global warming and 30 percent think it will threaten their lifestyle in their lifetime.

segments.title: Eco-psychology explanation and eco-therapy advice
segments.summary: Eco-psychologists see eco-anxiety as a byproduct of people's growing disconnection from the planet due to technology. Eco-therapists charge about $250 for fifty minutes and advise patients to carry a rock or bark or to go outside. The hosts question the value of this advice.

segments.title: Media influence and fear-based marketing
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how media, including An Inconvenient Truth, helped drive eco-anxiety. They explain that fear, uncertainty, and dread (FUD) are marketing tactics used to motivate people, and say environmental issues require more delicate handling.

segments.title: Useless information: scaring a vulture
segments.summary: Chuck presents a 'useless information' article by Kristen Conner explaining that scaring a vulture can make it vomit on cue, and that its vomit smells like dead things and burns.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to the articles on eco-anxiety and vultures on HowStuffWorks.com and invite email feedback.
